residue.text: Protected observation: B9 bears a ten-bracket packing mark but contains nine. Preserve its two-minute inspection, spare-bracket correction, recount and seal. The discrepancy cause is unknown and establishes no other discrepancy.

Suspected condition, not an observed mechanism: B9 retains its rack place during its longer inspection; whole-load unloading can block and occupy the transfer clerk. Make second trolley load size the control variable and rack headroom, unloading waits and occupied minutes the observables. Preserve the extra inspection minute even if no transfer penalty appears.

Proposed finite-model probe: inspect continuously from 0; trolley B4-B7 starts at 0. Compare trolley B8-B11 at 3 then hand B12 at 6, against trolley B8-B10 at 3 then hand B11 at 6 and B12 at 7. Record unload identities, rack occupancy, waits, charge, correct release times and both clerks occupied intervals. Rival A hypothesizes that the larger batch incurs waiting or sufficient added occupation to lose among complete successes. Rival B predicts early full-load unloading avoids blocking. Stage1 calculated prediction: both release twelve correctly by 13 without waits; transfer occupation is seven versus eight minutes, inspection thirteen in both. Defeat A if the full-load variant completes without waiting and uses fewer transfer minutes.

Nine source unloads and twelve correct releases are distinct outputs. Rank transfer occupation only among complete successes. One clerk serves each role; twelve seals and one spare bracket suffice. No extra resources or arrivals exist. No observed trials, performance distribution or global optimality proof are supplied. Later request adaptation is unobserved and cannot alter this window.

summary.text: Retain the anomalous B9 correction and test second-load size, four versus three, with the admitted early-transfer schedules. Continuous inspection from 0 is necessary because the required inspection work totals thirteen minutes. The closest rival claims that B9-related rack occupation reverses the larger-batch advantage; compare waiting and transfer burden while requiring twelve correct releases by 13.

Stage1 predicts equal complete releases and thirteen inspection minutes, with seven versus eight transfer minutes favoring the full second load. This is a finite-model calculation, not observed success or global optimality. Discrepancy causation and later request adaptation remain unknown.
